query: Why does having the orders service publish an event instead of calling shipping directly make the system easier to extend, and what does the orders service know about shipping?
expected_answer: The orders service has no knowledge that the shipping service exists; it just raises an 'Order Created' event. Because routing logic sits with the receiver, the shipping service controls whether it participates, which reduces coupling and adds pluggability.
expected_facts: orders service has no knowledge that the shipping service exists
receiver-driven routing places routing logic at the receiver

relevant_passages.quote: But there is an important change: the orders service has no knowledge that the shipping service exists.
This is an example of receiver-driven routing: logic for routing is located at the receiver of the events, rather than at the sender.

The advantage of orchestration is that the whole workflow is written down, in code, in one place, making it easy to reason about.
expected_facts: orchestration is tightly coupled to the controller
choreography suits larger implementations spanning teams
orchestration writes the whole workflow in one place in code

relevant_passages.quote: the advantage of orchestration is that the whole workflow is written down, in code, in one place. That makes it easy to reason about the system.

The downside is that the model is tightly coupled to the controller, so broadly speaking choreographed approaches better suit larger implementations (particularly those that span teams and hence change independently of one another).
